name: Jade Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. To start, could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead on the seaming and retort line at Greenvale Foods, a cannery that does beans, tomatoes and sweetcorn. In harvest season we run twelve-hour shifts, and I'm the one who checks every seam and every cooking cycle, because one bad seam can spoil a whole pallet. In winter the hours are shorter, and I train the seasonal workers who come back each year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm of harvest, when the whole valley is moving and the line hums for twelve hours. What wears me out is the heat from the retorts and the long shifts, and the feeling in January when the hours drop and the money gets tight. I've got a bad shoulder from lifting crates, and I try not to complain about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I'd expect. I'd say it at the church supper and at work, that new gadgets come and go and honest work stays. I'd tell the seasonal workers they've got nothing to worry about from a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm honest about it. The winter is what worries me, not AI. The hours drop in January and February, and we live on what we saved over harvest. My husband Anton manages an orchard and his pay's seasonal too, so we both have thin months, and about two months of savings isn't a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work the harvest, take every extra shift, and keep the winter training job with the seasonal crew. I'd make more jam and preserves from our own garden to sell at the farmers' market on Saturdays. And I'd put 120 a month into savings, because the thin months are never far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alright. A bit weary, but alright. A man who says he's never worried is lying, and a woman too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hours are seasonal. How does that feel for money in a quiet picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: January is the hard month. We cut back on everything, no extras, and the heating gets turned down. We've been fine so far, but one broken boiler or a car repair and we'd be using the credit card. That's what makes me careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools sometimes. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. My daughter Katya set me up with a chatbot, and I use it to put the line sheets into simple words for the seasonal workers who don't speak the local language well. It's good for that, and I always have one of the workers check my translated version.

say: I'd say new gadgets come and go, but **honest work** stays.
I'd tell the seasonal workers they've got nothing to fear from a **computer**.
think: The **winter** worries me more than AI, because hours drop in January and February.
Both Anton's and my pay are **seasonal**, and two months of savings isn't much.
do: Work the harvest and take every **extra shift**.
Sell more **jam and preserves** at the Saturday farmers' market.
feel: **Weary** but alright, and honest about having worries.
S0.quote: The winter is what worries me
fieldNote: **Seasonal money** is the real pressure, and AI barely registers.
**Steady with tools**: she uses a chatbot for translated line sheets and has workers check it.
**Home-grown side income** through preserves fits her values and her garden.

steps.text: Take every extra harvest shift at the cannery
Sell jam and preserves at the Saturday farmers' market
Keep translating line sheets with the chatbot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to keep our heads, work hard and learn what's proven to work. I'd say it at church and at the plant, and I'd say the firms that treat their people fairly will do better in the end. I'd also say I'm not against progress, just against being rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the plant gets cameras on the seams and software that plans the harvest, and the office shrinks. The retorts and the line get robots a bit later. I'm the lead, which means I do a lot of planning, and some of that could go to a screen, so I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant to put me on the new camera inspection trial, because someone on the floor needs to know it. I'd also train a couple of the seasonal workers to be reliable regulars, so the plant has people it can count on. And I'd save another 100 a month, aiming for four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary and curious, both. It reminds me of when they changed the old seaming machine, and we all thought it would go badly, but it was better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks on your line would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning the harvest schedule and ordering the cans and labels are the first jobs I can see going to software. Also the paperwork for the food safety checks, which is already half on computers. The seam checking, I can see cameras doing it better than my eyes at hour eleven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the seasonal workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn how the new camera works, and to be dependable, because a plant needs people it can count on. I'd also tell them that if they do their job well, a good lead like me will put in a word for them.

say: I'd say keep our heads, work hard and learn what's **proven to work**.
Firms that treat their people **fairly** will do better in the end.
think: The plant gets **cameras** on the seams and software for planning, and the office shrinks.
Some of my **lead planning** could go to a screen, so I'd be watching.
do: Ask to join the **camera inspection** trial at the plant.
Train a few seasonal workers to be **reliable regulars**.
Save another **100 a month** to reach four months.
feel: **Wary and curious**, like when the old seaming machine was replaced and it turned out better.
fieldNote: **Steady temperament**: she says she's not against progress, only against being rushed.
**Loyalty** to the seasonal workers shapes her actions.
**Her planning duties** are the part she thinks will move to software.

steps.text: Ask to join the plant's camera seam inspection trial
Save an extra 100 a month for four months of cushion
Train the best seasonal workers to return every year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be calm and practical, and I'd say prayers are not a plan. I'd say the plant, the church and the community should sit together. Two years is not enough for politicians, so we'd have to do it ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared, I won't pretend. The planning and ordering go in 2028, and Greenvale is a small plant that might close or sell to a bigger one. The robots would come by 2031, and I'd be 63, too young to stop and too old for anyone to hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Anton that night and cut everything we can. I'd save up to six months, using the harvest money. I'd also ask the plant if I can be the lead for a robot line, and I'd start selling more preserves, maybe at the town market too. Whatever happens, I'd want an income that doesn't depend on one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd be quiet at the table and the family would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about 2031. What does that mean for your own line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, because the robots take three years to match what I do. A plant doesn't wait, and Greenvale could sell to a larger company that brings its own machines and its own team. Then my three years would shrink to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Katya to keep her bookkeeping job and learn the tools that read invoices, since she'll work with them. And I'd tell my son Pavel the mechanic that machines need people who can fix them. I'd tell them both we'll be alright, and that faith and family are what we have.

say: I'd say be **calm and practical**, and the plant, church and community should sit together.
Two years is not enough for politicians, so we'd do it **ourselves**.
think: Greenvale is small and might **close or sell** to a bigger company.
By 2031 I'd be 63, too young to stop and too old for anyone to **hire**.
do: Talk to Anton that night and **cut everything** we can.
Use the harvest money to build **six months** of savings.
Ask to lead a **robot line** and sell more preserves at the town market.
feel: **Heavy**, quiet at the table, and the family would notice.
fieldNote: **Anxious** because a small plant can be sold, and her three-year gap could shrink to one.
**Diversify income**: she wants income that doesn't hang on one employer.

steps.text: Cut everything possible at home that same week
Use harvest earnings to build six months of savings
Sell preserves at the town market as well as the farmers' market
Ask to lead the first robot-run line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and it's up to each of us to use it. I'd tell the workers to save and learn a second skill. Hard work and good habits still count, but nobody should wait for the plant to tell them what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd be fairly comfortable. I'd be 63 when AI arrives and 66 when robots reach the line, and I'd plan to be retired before that. The people I worry about are the young seasonal workers, who rely on the plant for half their year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 62 and clear the small loan on the car. I'd set aside 200 a month and reach six months of savings in three years. I'd also grow the preserves business a bit, with a proper stall and a name on the jars, as something Anton and I can do together in retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. I can plan for this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what do you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think government should do what it does best, which is keep the rules fair and help with retraining and apprenticeships. It shouldn't take over from families and firms. But if a plant closes and a whole valley loses its work, the community needs a bridge, and the government should help build it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you see the role of the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Using the first two years to save and the next three to get the preserves business to a proper state. And I'd train a successor on the line, so I'm leaving it in good hands.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning**, and each of us must use it.
I'd tell workers to save and learn a **second skill**.
think: I'd be fairly **comfortable**, planning to retire before robots reach the line in 2034.
I worry about **young seasonal workers** who rely on the plant for half their year.
do: Work until **62** and clear the small car loan.
Set aside **200 a month** to reach six months of savings.
Grow the **preserves business** with a proper stall and named jars.
feel: **Steadier**, because this one I can plan for.
fieldNote: **Planful**: five years turns anxiety into specific targets.
**Values-led view of government**: fair rules and a bridge, not takeover.
**Retirement plan** includes a shared preserves business with her husband.

steps.text: Work until 62 and clear the car loan
Save 200 a month to reach six months in the bank
Build a proper preserves stall with a name on the jars

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a gift, as long as people use it wisely. I'd say we've got time to train the young in trades the machines need, and time for families to be ready. That's the best way to face any big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be 68 and retired, so I'm fine. The thing on my mind is the valley. Greenvale employs a few hundred people in season, and if it shrinks, the shops and the school feel it. I'd want the church and the council to talk early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire around 62 and put more time into the preserves stall, and into church and the grandchildren. I'd probably still help at the plant for a few weeks at harvest if they want me. And I'd keep my savings steady and not take risks with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd be at peace, and I'd feel for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you well past retirement. What stays on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the machine and also the screens, because the person who understands both is the one who stays. And be dependable, because a good name carries further than any skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell somebody just starting in a cannery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd say hold on to a trade that needs hands. Machines will do a lot, but a valley still needs people who can fix, grow and build.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, as long as people use it wisely.
There's time to train the young in **trades** the machines need.
think: For me it's **fine**, since I'd be 68 and retired.
My concern is the **valley**, because if Greenvale shrinks, the shops and the school feel it.
do: Retire around **62** and put more time into the preserves stall.
Help at the plant for a few **harvest weeks** if they want me.
feel: **Calm** and at peace, but feeling for the young ones.
fieldNote: **Secure and settled**: long timeline plus retirement plan leave her calm.
**Advice**: learn the machine and the screens, and keep a good name.

steps.text: Retire around 62 and run the preserves stall more
Help at the plant for a few harvest weeks each year
Keep savings in plain, steady accounts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because a small plant can be sold, and my hands-on years could shrink to one. What would help is the plant being honest with us, retraining that pays while we learn, and a pension that doesn't penalise me for leaving a bit early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the seasonal workers. Some of the seasonal workers have worked beside me for fifteen years. If the plant goes, they go first, and nobody will notice.

portrait: **Jade** is a 58-year-old line lead at a vegetable cannery with seasonal hours, a few years from retirement.
She is traditional and steady, uses a chatbot now and then, and values **work, family and community** over handouts.
Her husband's orchard pay is seasonal too, so about **two months** of savings matter a great deal.
She stays uneasy in most pictures and turns **anxious** where a small plant could be sold or closed early.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because a small plant can be sold and her hands-on years could shrink.
whatWouldHelp: An **honest plant**, retraining that pays while she learns, and a pension that doesn't penalise early leavers.
